title: Message queues
summary: How a queue lets one service hand work to another without waiting, absorbs bursts, and makes sure each job is done even if a worker crashes.

blocks.p: A user uploads a video. The app has to resize it, make thumbnails and send an email. Doing all of that inside the request takes minutes, and the user waits the whole time.

Traffic is also uneven. A sale or a news story can bring several times the usual load for a few minutes. If every request needs a worker straight away, you need enough workers for the worst minute of the year, or requests fail during it.

A **message queue** sits between a **producer**, the service that has work to hand off, and **consumers**, the workers that do it. The producer puts a message on the queue and moves on. Consumers take messages off when they are ready.

The two sides no longer have to run at the same speed. During a burst the queue grows. When the burst ends, consumers keep working and the queue drains. With a durable queue that keeps messages until they are processed, nothing is lost, but messages wait longer while the queue is long.

blocks.caption: Two consumers handle about 4 messages a second. For 3 seconds, 9 a second arrive. The queue grows, then drains after the burst.

blocks.p: Several consumers can read from one queue. Each message goes to only one of them, so adding consumers adds throughput. This is the usual way to scale background work.

blocks.caption: Three consumers share one queue. Each message is handed to one of them at a time. If a consumer fails before acknowledging it, the queue hands it to another.

blocks.p: A consumer that crashes halfway through a job must not lose it. So the queue doesn't delete a message when it hands it out. The consumer **acknowledges** it after the work is done, and only then is it removed.
If no acknowledgement arrives in time, the queue hands the message to another consumer. This means a message can be processed twice, which the delivery guarantees lesson covers.
A message that fails every time, such as one with bad data, would be retried forever. Queues move it to a **dead-letter queue** after a set number of attempts, so someone can look at it later.
Each consumer takes about half a second per message. Change the number of consumers and the burst rate, and watch how long messages wait.

blocks.caption: A burst from 3 to 6 seconds. With too few consumers the queue keeps growing until the burst ends.

list: **SQS hides a message while it is worked on.** Amazon SQS uses a [visibility timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html). The consumer must delete the message before it ends, or the message becomes visible to other consumers again.

**Dead-letter queues are built in.** SQS moves a message to a [dead-letter queue](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html) after it has been received a set number of times.

**RabbitMQ uses explicit acks.** RabbitMQ's [consumer acknowledgements](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms) let a consumer confirm each message, and requeue messages from a consumer whose connection drops.
**Watch the age of the oldest message.** Queue length alone can mislead. The age of the oldest message tells you how far behind consumers are, and is a good signal for adding consumers.
A queue lets a producer hand off work and move on, while consumers work at their own pace.
Bursts make the queue grow instead of failing requests. Messages wait longer until it drains.
Several consumers can share a queue, and each message goes to one of them.
Consumers acknowledge a message after the work is done, so a crash doesn't lose it. Repeated failures go to a dead-letter queue.
